weeks.title: The Fundamentals of Good Writing
weeks.overview:
Welcome back to your Content Writing journey. Last week you were introduced to content writing, explored the different roles and opportunities within the field, and learned how to identify your audience and determine the purpose of your writing. Those lessons gave you the foundation you need to begin thinking like a content writer.

Now we get into the real work. This is the second and final week of your probation phase, and we are moving beyond introductions into the actual craft of writing. You will learn how to make your writing clearer, structure your sentences and paragraphs effectively, communicate naturally, eliminate unnecessary words, and make your ideas easier for readers to understand.

These are not skills you will use once and forget. They are principles you will apply throughout your entire journey as a content writer, regardless of the type of content you eventually specialise in.
weeks.objectives:
By the end of this week you should be able to:

1. Communicate ideas clearly and simply, and explain why good writing does not need to sound complicated to be intelligent.
2. Remove unnecessary words, and avoid repeating the same point without reason.
3. Construct sentences that communicate complete thoughts and read naturally.
4. Organise your ideas into paragraphs that are coherent and easy to follow.
5. Recognise active and passive voice, and choose deliberately between them.
6. Apply the principle of showing rather than telling to make your writing more vivid.
7. Write conversationally and naturally without abandoning clarity or care.
8. Vary your sentence length and structure to give your writing rhythm.

This is the final week of your probation phase. Your assignments will be more demanding than last week's, and your assessment will bring together what you have learned across both weeks. To progress beyond the probation phase, you need to achieve a minimum score of 60% in your probation assessment.

lessons.title: Welcome Back — The Fundamentals of Good Writing
lessons.content:
Welcome back to your Content Writing journey!

Last week, we covered the basics. You were introduced to content writing, explored the different roles and opportunities within the field, and learned how to identify your audience and determine the purpose of your writing.

Those lessons gave you the foundation you need to begin thinking like a content writer.

But now, we're getting into the real work.

This is the second and final week of your probation phase, and we're moving beyond introductions into the actual craft of writing. It's time to understand what separates writing that merely communicates something from writing that communicates it exceptionally well.

Today, we're focusing on the fundamentals of good writing.

You'll learn how to make your writing clearer, structure your sentences and paragraphs effectively, communicate naturally, eliminate unnecessary words, and make your ideas easier for readers to understand.

And here's something important: these aren't skills you'll use once and forget. They are principles you'll apply throughout your entire journey as a content writer, regardless of the type of content you eventually specialise in.

lessons.title: Important — Your Final Probation Week
lessons.content:
This is the final week of your probation phase.

Your assignments will be more demanding than those from last week, and your assessment will bring together what you've learned across both weeks.

You will also be required to put your understanding of good writing into practice. It's no longer enough to watch a video, understand an explanation, and move on. You must be able to demonstrate what you've learned through your own writing.

To progress beyond the probation phase, you need to achieve a minimum score of 60% in your probation assessment.

That means you need to pay attention, take your lessons seriously, and practise what you're learning.

For today's class, make sure you have your notebook and a pen ready. The first lesson will revisit some foundational principles, but the lessons that follow will take you deeper into the craft.

Take notes as you watch each video. Record important principles, examples, techniques, and anything you can apply to your own writing.

Don't just watch these lessons. Study them.

lessons.title: What You'll Learn Today
lessons.content:
Today's lesson covers the following areas:

1. Clarity, Simplicity, and Concise Writing
2. Writing Better Sentences
3. Writing Better Paragraphs
4. Active vs Passive Voice
5. Show, Don't Tell
6. Writing Conversationally
7. Writing Rhythm and Sentence Variety

Work through each part below in order. Each part has a short overview, then the full lesson video to watch.

lessons.title: Part 1 — Clarity, Simplicity & Concise Writing
lessons.content:
Let's begin with one of the most important principles of good writing: making your message easy to understand.

Good writing doesn't have to sound complicated to be intelligent. In fact, a writer who can communicate a complex idea in simple, clear language demonstrates a valuable skill.

Your job is not to impress readers with unnecessarily complicated vocabulary or long sentences. Your job is to communicate your message effectively.

This means learning to express ideas clearly, choose words carefully, remove unnecessary words, avoid repeating the same point without a reason, and make your writing easy to follow.

Remember, readers shouldn't have to struggle to understand what you're trying to say.

As you watch this first lesson, pay attention to how clarity and simplicity improve writing, and how unnecessary words can weaken an otherwise good piece of content.

lessons.title: Part 2 — Writing Better Sentences
lessons.content:
Now that you understand the importance of clear and concise writing, it's time to look at how you construct your sentences.

Sentences are the building blocks of your writing. If your sentences are confusing, awkward, incomplete, or poorly structured, your readers may struggle to understand even a good idea.

Learning to write better sentences involves understanding how words work together, how to communicate complete thoughts, and how to express your ideas in a way that feels natural and easy to follow.

As you progress, you'll discover that writing a good sentence isn't simply about following grammatical rules. It's also about knowing how to communicate your intended meaning effectively.

lessons.title: Part 3 — Writing Better Paragraphs
lessons.content:
Good sentences are important, but sentences don't exist in isolation. They come together to form paragraphs, and those paragraphs help organise your ideas into a coherent piece of writing.

A well-structured paragraph helps readers understand the point you're making, follow your reasoning, and move naturally from one idea to the next.

In this lesson, you'll explore how paragraphs work and how to organise your thoughts so your writing feels connected rather than scattered.

Pay attention to how individual ideas fit together and how paragraph structure influences the reading experience.

lessons.title: Part 4 — Active vs Passive Voice
lessons.content:
Another important aspect of writing is understanding how you construct your sentences to communicate actions and ideas.

Active and passive voice offer different ways of presenting information. Understanding the difference helps you make deliberate choices about how you communicate, what you emphasise, and how direct your writing feels.

This is particularly important when you want your writing to be clear, direct, and easy to follow.

As you watch this lesson, focus on understanding both forms and recognising when one may be more appropriate than the other.

lessons.title: Part 5 — Show, Don't Tell
lessons.content:
Here's another principle you'll encounter frequently as you develop your writing skills: show, don't tell.

The way you communicate an idea can determine how your reader experiences it.

Sometimes, simply stating something isn't as effective as using specific details, descriptions, examples, or actions that help the reader understand and experience what you're communicating.

This principle is particularly useful in storytelling, descriptive writing, personal experiences, and other forms of content where you want to create a stronger connection with your reader.

In this lesson, pay attention to the difference between merely telling readers something and presenting it in a way that allows them to understand it more vividly.

lessons.title: Part 6 — Writing Conversationally
lessons.content:
Good writing doesn't always have to sound formal or academic.

Depending on your audience, platform, and purpose, your writing may need to feel natural, warm, engaging, and conversational.

Think about how people communicate in everyday conversations. They want to understand one another without feeling as though they're reading a complicated instruction manual.

Conversational writing aims to create that sense of natural communication while still being clear, intentional, and appropriate for the reader.

This doesn't mean abandoning grammar or writing carelessly. It means learning how to communicate in a way that feels natural rather than unnecessarily stiff.

You'll explore this further in the following lesson.

lessons.title: Part 6 — Writing Conversationally — Part 2
lessons.content:
This lesson continues the topic of writing conversationally.

Watch it in full before moving on to the final part of today's lesson.

lessons.title: Part 7 — Rhythm in Writing
lessons.content:
Finally, let's talk about rhythm.

Have you ever read something that felt smooth, natural, and enjoyable, only to encounter another piece of writing that felt repetitive or exhausting?

The rhythm of writing can influence that experience.

Sentence length, word choice, punctuation, and the way ideas flow together can all affect the pace at which readers experience your writing.

Using sentences of the same length and structure repeatedly can make your writing feel monotonous. Learning to vary your sentences can help create a more engaging reading experience.

In this lesson, you'll explore writing rhythm and begin understanding how the flow of your words affects the way your content feels to the reader.

lessons.title: Monday's Goal
lessons.content:
Today, your goal is to move beyond simply understanding what content writing is and begin learning how to write well.

By the end of this lesson, you should have a better understanding of how to:

- Communicate ideas clearly and simply.
- Remove unnecessary words and avoid needless repetition.
- Construct better sentences and paragraphs.
- Understand and use active and passive voice appropriately.
- Make your writing more vivid through the principle of showing rather than telling.
- Write naturally and conversationally.
- Improve the rhythm and flow of your writing.

However, watching these videos is only the beginning. The real progress happens when you start applying what you've learned to your own work.

As you watch, don't just write down definitions. Pay attention to the examples. Notice what makes one sentence stronger than another, what makes a paragraph easier to follow, and how small changes can improve an entire piece of writing.

Remember, this is your final week of probation. Your upcoming assignments will challenge you to demonstrate what you've learned across both weeks.

Take your notes. Study the lessons. Pay attention to the details. And, most importantly, practise.

It's time to move from knowing about writing to developing the ability to write well.

lessons.title: Tuesday — Finding Your Writing Voice
lessons.content:
Welcome back, writers!

In our last class, we explored the fundamentals of good writing: clarity, simplicity, sentence structure, paragraph structure, rhythm, and how to make our writing easier to understand.

Today, we're going a step further.

Knowing how to write correctly is one thing. Knowing how to write in a way that sounds like you is another.

Think about it. Have you ever read something and immediately felt the personality behind the words? Perhaps the writer was funny, bold, thoughtful, emotional, or incredibly good at telling stories. Even without seeing the person, you could almost imagine what they might sound like in a conversation.

That's the power of a writing voice.

Today, we'll explore how writers develop their unique voices, how voice differs from tone, and how to write in a way that feels natural, authentic, and recognisably human.

A quick reminder: This is the final week of your probation phase. The assignments are becoming more demanding, and your assessment will cover what you've learned across both weeks. You need a minimum score of 60% to progress to the next phase.

Please have your dedicated Content Writing notebook and a pen ready. Take notes as you watch the videos, reflect on the concepts, and pay attention to the writing around you. Don't just watch to finish the lesson. Watch to understand and practise.

Let's get into it!

lessons.title: What You'll Learn Today — Finding Your Writing Voice
lessons.content:
By the end of today's lesson, you should understand:

- What a writing voice is and why it matters.
- The difference between voice and tone.
- Different writing styles and how they communicate personality.
- How to begin developing your own writing voice.
- How to maintain consistency across your writing.
- What it means to write like a human.
- How to recognise and avoid generic, AI-sounding writing.

Work through each part below in order.

lessons.title: Part 1 — Understanding Your Writing Voice
lessons.content:
Before you can develop your writing voice, you need to understand what it actually means.

Your writing voice is the distinctive personality, perspective, and character that comes through in your writing.

It is the way your words sound to a reader, even when you're not physically present to speak them.

Two people can write about the same subject, communicate the same message, and use correct grammar, yet produce completely different experiences for their readers.

Imagine two writers discussing the importance of discipline.

Writer A:

"Discipline is an essential component of personal development. Individuals who consistently practise discipline are more likely to achieve their goals and maintain productive habits."

Writer B:

"Let's be honest. You probably don't need another motivational video. You need to do the thing you promised yourself you'd do three days ago."

Both writers are communicating a similar idea. However, their writing feels different.

The first sounds formal, structured, and educational. The second sounds direct, conversational, and slightly confrontational.

Neither approach is automatically better. Their effectiveness depends on the audience, the purpose, and the experience the writer wants to create.

The difference is that each writer communicates through a different voice.

WHAT MAKES UP A WRITING VOICE?

Your writing voice can be shaped by several things:

- Your word choices: Do you use simple, everyday language or more technical vocabulary?
- Your perspective: Do you approach subjects like a teacher, storyteller, researcher, comedian, or challenger?
- Your personality: Are you naturally playful, serious, curious, direct, reflective, or expressive?
- Your sentence patterns: Do you prefer short, punchy statements or longer, thoughtful explanations?
- Your way of thinking: Do you challenge popular beliefs, explain complicated ideas, ask difficult questions, or explore personal experiences?
- Your relationship with the reader: Do you sound like a friend having a conversation, a professional sharing expertise, or a storyteller taking someone on a journey?

These elements work together to give your writing its character.

DOES EVERYONE ALREADY HAVE A WRITING VOICE?

You may already have the beginnings of a writing voice in the way you speak, think, explain things, tell stories, and express your opinions.

However, your writing voice doesn't necessarily emerge fully formed. It develops through practice, experimentation, reading, observation, and discovering how you naturally communicate.

You might start by imitating certain writing styles you admire. As you gain experience, you begin to understand what feels natural to you and what doesn't.

The goal isn't to manufacture a personality for your writing. It's to develop a deliberate way of expressing yourself through words.

Watch the video below to learn more about finding and developing your writing voice. As you watch, pay attention to how a writer discovers what feels natural, experiments with different approaches, and develops a distinctive style.

lessons.title: Part 1 — Finding Your Writing Voice — Continued Learning
lessons.content:
This second video continues the topic of finding and developing your writing voice.

As you watch, pay attention to how a writer discovers what feels natural, experiments with different approaches, and develops a distinctive style.

Take notes on anything you can apply to your own writing.

lessons.title: Part 2 — Tone vs. Voice: Understanding the Difference
lessons.content:
This is one of the most important distinctions in today's lesson.

Writers sometimes use the words voice and tone interchangeably, but they are not the same thing.

Voice is the personality behind your writing. Tone is the attitude or emotional quality your writing communicates in a particular situation.

Think of it this way:

Your voice is who you sound like.

Your tone is how you sound in a particular moment.

Imagine you have a friend who is naturally funny, playful, and expressive. That's part of their personality. However, when they attend a funeral, they won't approach the situation with the same humour they use when joking with friends.

Their personality hasn't disappeared. They've simply adjusted how they express themselves to suit the situation.

Writing works similarly.

Your voice can remain recognisable while your tone changes depending on what you're writing, who you're addressing, and what you want to communicate.

Let's use an example.

Imagine you're a content writer whose natural writing voice is conversational, direct, and slightly humorous. You write social media posts, educational articles, personal stories, and professional emails.

Your underlying voice may remain recognisable across all these formats, but the tone will change.

Example 1: Educational tone

"Before you publish your next article, identify the central message you want readers to remember. This will help you organise your ideas and eliminate unnecessary information."

The tone is instructive and informative.

Example 2: Humorous tone

"You've written 2,000 words, but somehow your article still hasn't answered the question you started with. Let's fix that."

The tone is playful and slightly teasing.

Example 3: Serious and reflective tone

"Sometimes, we write so much because we're afraid that saying less will make our ideas seem less important. But clarity often begins when we learn what to leave out."

The tone is thoughtful and serious.

Example 4: Encouraging tone

"You don't need to sound like an award-winning author today. Start by making one idea clear. Then make the next one clearer. That's how you improve."

The tone is supportive and reassuring.

Notice what happens here.

The writer can maintain a conversational, direct style while changing the tone to suit the message.

That's the relationship between voice and tone.

WHY DOES TONE CHANGE?

Tone changes because different situations require different kinds of communication.

You wouldn't write a condolence message the same way you'd write a funny social media post. You wouldn't explain a serious financial problem with the same attitude you'd use to describe a weekend adventure.

Your tone should respond to factors such as:

1. Your audience

Who are you speaking to? What do they know? What do they need from you? What kind of language will help them understand and connect with your message?

2. Your purpose

Are you trying to educate, entertain, persuade, comfort, challenge, encourage, or inform? Your purpose influences how your words should feel.

3. Your subject

Some subjects naturally require more sensitivity or seriousness than others. A personal tragedy calls for a different tone from a lighthearted story about an embarrassing experience.

4. The platform or format

A LinkedIn article, an Instagram caption, a formal business email, and a personal newsletter may require different tones, even when written by the same person.

5. The reader's emotional state

Someone seeking help with a difficult problem may need a calm and reassuring tone. Someone reading a motivational piece may respond better to bold, energetic language.

CAN YOUR VOICE CHANGE?

Yes. Your writing voice can evolve as you learn, mature, gain experience, and discover new ways of expressing yourself.

However, there's a difference between allowing your voice to develop and changing your personality completely every time you write.

You don't need to sound like an entirely different person on every platform. A writer can become more skilled, more thoughtful, and more versatile while still maintaining a recognisable identity.

A SIMPLE WAY TO REMEMBER THE DIFFERENCE

Think about a musician.

The musician has a recognisable style, character, and way of expressing music. That's similar to voice.

However, the musician can perform a joyful song, a heartbreaking ballad, or an intense anthem. The emotional feeling of each performance changes, but the musician's identity can still come through.

That's similar to tone.

Voice gives your writing its identity. Tone helps you express the right attitude for the moment.

Understanding this distinction will help you become a more flexible writer without losing your individuality.

lessons.title: Part 3 — Different Writing Styles and Expressions
lessons.content:
As you work towards discovering your writing voice, you'll encounter different ways of expressing ideas.

Some writers are naturally educational. Others tell compelling stories, make people laugh, challenge assumptions, or communicate emotion exceptionally well.

These approaches aren't necessarily permanent categories. A single writer can use several of them, sometimes within the same piece.

The important thing is understanding how different approaches work and learning which ones suit your personality, audience, and purpose.

EDUCATIONAL WRITING

Educational writing focuses on helping readers understand something. It breaks down ideas, explains concepts, answers questions, and makes information easier to learn.

For example:

"Your opening paragraph should introduce the central idea of your article. It gives readers an initial understanding of what to expect and helps them decide whether to continue reading."

This approach prioritises clarity, explanation, and understanding. It is useful for tutorials, educational social media posts, articles, guides, and learning materials.

HUMOROUS WRITING

Humorous writing uses wit, irony, exaggeration, unexpected observations, or playful language to entertain readers.

For example:

"I opened my laptop to write one paragraph. Three hours later, I had reorganised my entire life, watched seven videos, and written absolutely nothing."

Humour can make writing memorable and relatable. However, good humour isn't simply adding jokes everywhere. It requires understanding your audience, timing, context, and what people will find amusing.

EMOTIONAL WRITING

Emotional writing helps readers feel something. It might communicate joy, grief, fear, hope, disappointment, love, frustration, or vulnerability.

For example:

"I kept telling everyone I was fine because I didn't know how to explain that I was tired of trying so hard and still feeling like I wasn't getting anywhere."

This kind of writing can help readers recognise their own experiences in someone else's words. The goal isn't to force emotion into every sentence. It's to express experiences, thoughts, and feelings in a way that feels honest and meaningful.

BOLD WRITING

Bold writing communicates ideas with confidence, conviction, and directness. It can challenge assumptions, question accepted beliefs, or encourage readers to confront uncomfortable truths.

For example:

"Your problem might not be that you lack potential. It might be that you've spent years protecting your potential from the possibility of failure."

Bold writing can attract attention and provoke thought. However, being bold doesn't mean being unnecessarily aggressive, insulting people, or making claims you cannot support. Confidence works best when it is backed by clear reasoning and a meaningful point.

STORYTELLING WRITING

Storytelling writing communicates through experiences, events, characters, conflict, and change. Rather than simply presenting a lesson, it takes readers through an experience that helps them discover the lesson.

For example:

"I spent three months preparing to start writing online. I bought notebooks, saved tutorials, and planned my content calendar. Then, one Monday morning, I realised I had done everything except publish a single post."

The writer could simply say, "Preparation without action is procrastination." But the story allows readers to experience the idea before reaching the conclusion.

Storytelling is especially useful when you want to make an abstract idea relatable, communicate personal experiences, or help readers remember a message.

FORMAL AND PROFESSIONAL WRITING

Formal and professional writing prioritises appropriate language, clarity, structure, and respect for the situation.

For example:

"Please find attached the revised proposal for your review. I would appreciate your feedback before the end of the week."

This is appropriate for many professional communications. However, formal and professional writing are not always identical. Professional writing can also be warm, conversational, and simple. You don't have to make your writing unnecessarily complicated to sound professional.

CONVERSATIONAL WRITING

Conversational writing sounds natural and approachable, as though the writer is speaking directly to the reader.

For example:

"Before you start writing, take a minute to figure out what you actually want to say. It'll save you a lot of unnecessary editing later."

It often uses familiar language, direct address, and natural sentence patterns. But conversational writing isn't the same as careless writing. It still needs structure, clarity, and an understanding of the reader.

WHAT SHOULD YOU TAKE AWAY FROM THIS?

You don't have to choose exactly one of these approaches and use it forever.

A writer might use storytelling to introduce an idea, educational writing to explain it, bold writing to challenge a misconception, and a conversational tone to make the entire piece approachable.

The question isn't simply, "Which writing style am I?"

A better question is:

"Which ways of expressing ideas feel natural to me, and which approaches best serve the message I'm trying to communicate?"

Your answers will help you discover and develop your writing voice.

lessons.title: Part 4 — Developing a Consistent Writing Voice
lessons.content:
Discovering your writing voice is one thing. Maintaining it is another.

Imagine following a writer whose posts are usually thoughtful, honest, and conversational. One day, their writing sounds like a friend sharing an interesting discovery. The next day, it sounds like a generic corporate brochure. The day after that, it becomes unnecessarily dramatic.

The variation may leave readers unsure of what to expect.

Consistency helps readers become familiar with the experience your writing offers. It allows them to recognise your approach, understand your personality, and develop a stronger connection with your work.

HOW DO YOU DEVELOP CONSISTENCY?

1. Identify the qualities you want your writing to communicate.

Think about how you want readers to experience your writing. Do you want to sound curious, thoughtful, humorous, direct, reassuring, analytical, or bold?

Choose a few qualities that genuinely reflect you or the identity you're deliberately developing as a writer. You don't need twenty adjectives. Start with two or three.

2. Pay attention to how you naturally communicate.

Observe how you explain things to friends, express opinions, tell stories, or discuss subjects that interest you. Do you ask questions? Do you use analogies? Do you challenge assumptions? Do you explain ideas step by step?

These habits may reveal useful clues about your natural voice.

3. Study writers you admire.

Read their articles, newsletters, social media posts, and other written work. Pay attention to how they use words, structure their sentences, introduce ideas, tell stories, and communicate emotion.

Learn from their techniques without assuming you must become a copy of them.

4. Practise writing regularly.

Your voice becomes clearer through use. Write about different subjects. Experiment with different approaches. Review your work and identify the patterns that feel most natural.

You don't have to wait until you've discovered your perfect voice before you start writing. Often, you discover it by writing.

5. Review your previous work.

Look through several pieces you've written. What similarities do you notice? Which pieces sound most natural? Which ones feel forced? What do you consistently do well?

This helps you recognise your emerging writing habits and decide which ones to develop.

6. Adapt without losing your identity.

Remember our discussion about tone. Your tone can change to suit different audiences and situations while your underlying voice remains recognisable.

Consistency doesn't mean using the same sentence structure, emotional intensity, or vocabulary in every piece. It means maintaining a recognisable approach to communicating.

lessons.title: Part 5 — Writing Like a Human: Avoiding Generic AI-Sounding Writing
lessons.content:
Let's talk about something particularly important for modern content writers.

Artificial intelligence can help generate, organise, and refine written content. But the availability of AI tools has also made it easier to produce writing that sounds polished while saying very little.

You've probably encountered writing that uses impressive words, perfectly arranged paragraphs, and motivational statements but leaves you wondering what the writer actually meant.

It sounds like writing. It may even be grammatically correct.

Yet it feels generic, impersonal, or strangely lifeless.

This is one of the reasons developing your own writing voice matters.

WHAT MAKES WRITING FEEL GENERIC?

Generic writing often relies on familiar phrases, predictable structures, broad statements, and ideas that could have been written by almost anyone.

For example:

"In today's fast-paced digital world, it is more important than ever to unlock your full potential and embrace the power of innovation."

What does this actually tell us? Very little. Which digital world? What potential? What kind of innovation? Why does it matter to the reader?

The sentence sounds polished, but it lacks specificity.

Now consider this:

"You've watched twenty tutorials on content creation, but you still haven't published your first post. At some point, you have to stop collecting information and start using it."

The second version is more specific. It presents a recognisable situation, identifies a problem, and communicates a clear point. It feels more human because it gives the reader something concrete to recognise or think about.

COMMON SIGNS OF GENERIC, AI-SOUNDING WRITING

1. Empty generalisations

Statements such as "success requires hard work" or "consistency is the key to growth" may be true, but they are often too broad to be useful on their own.

Instead of repeating a familiar statement, explore what it means in a specific situation. For example, rather than simply saying, "Consistency is important," explain what consistency looks like when someone is trying to develop a writing habit.

2. Overused expressions

Phrases such as "in today's fast-paced world," "unlock your full potential," and "embark on a journey" can become predictable when used without a clear reason.

These expressions aren't automatically wrong. The problem is relying on familiar language when a more precise expression would communicate the idea better.

3. Unnecessary complexity

Sometimes, writers use long words and elaborate sentences to make simple ideas sound impressive.

For example:

"It is imperative that individuals prioritise the implementation of effective communication strategies."

A clearer alternative might be:

"People need to communicate more effectively."

Choose language that serves the idea rather than language that merely makes it sound sophisticated.

4. Predictable motivational language

Statements such as "Believe in yourself, stay focused, and never give up" may sound encouraging, but they rarely offer anything distinctive without further explanation.

What should the reader believe in? What should they focus on? What should they do when they feel like giving up? Specificity makes encouragement more meaningful.

5. Repetition without development

Repeating the same idea in several different ways can make writing feel longer without making it more valuable. Once you've communicated a point clearly, ask whether the next sentence adds something new. If it doesn't, consider removing it.

6. A lack of specific details

Generic writing often describes experiences in broad terms without showing what actually happened.

Compare:

"I learned an important lesson about perseverance."

With:

"I rewrote the introduction six times before I realised the problem wasn't my vocabulary. I hadn't decided what I wanted the reader to understand."

The second example gives the reader a specific experience to engage with.

7. A voice that doesn't feel natural

If you normally communicate in simple, direct language, forcing yourself to write like an academic textbook may make your writing feel unnatural. Likewise, forcing jokes, slang, dramatic statements, or emotional language into every paragraph can make your writing feel artificial.

The goal is not to make your writing casual at all costs. It is to make your expression appropriate, natural, and intentional.

HOW DO YOU MAKE YOUR WRITING FEEL MORE HUMAN?

Start with what you actually want to say.

Before worrying about sounding impressive, identify the central idea you want to communicate. Explain it in the clearest language you can.

Be specific.

Use concrete examples, meaningful details, and observations that help readers understand what you mean. Instead of telling readers that failure teaches important lessons, describe what a particular failure revealed and how it changed your approach.

Allow yourself to have a perspective.

You don't need to make every piece controversial, but your writing should communicate a meaningful point of view. What do you believe? What have you observed? What do you question? What do you understand differently from the way you did before? A perspective gives your writing direction.

Use natural language.

Write in a way that feels appropriate for your audience and your personality. Read your sentences aloud. If they sound unnecessarily complicated or unlike anything you would naturally say, reconsider them.

Use stories and observations when they genuinely add value.

Specific experiences can help readers connect with ideas. But don't invent personal experiences or pretend to have feelings and memories you don't have just to make a piece more engaging. Honesty matters.

Edit for meaning, not just grammar.

Correct grammar is important, but proofreading should go beyond correcting errors. Ask yourself:

- Is my point clear?
- Does this sentence add anything?
- Is this the most natural way to express the idea?
- Have I explained what I actually mean?
- Could this sentence apply to almost any person, business, or situation?
- Have I included anything specific that makes this piece meaningful?

WHAT ABOUT USING AI AS A WRITER?

Using AI does not automatically make your writing generic or inauthentic. AI can help you brainstorm, organise ideas, identify grammatical errors, explore alternative expressions, or improve clarity.

The problem arises when you rely on it to do all the thinking and accept its output without examining whether the content reflects your intended message, perspective, and voice.

If you use AI, treat its output as material to evaluate rather than something you must accept exactly as it appears. Ask yourself whether the writing communicates what you actually mean. Replace vague statements with specific ideas. Remove unnecessary language. Check the accuracy of its claims. Refine the tone and make sure the final piece serves the reader.

And when a task requires your independent writing, follow the instructions. For this course, your ability to think and write for yourself is part of what you're learning.

Remember: the goal isn't to make your writing sound human by adding random slang or making deliberate grammatical mistakes. The goal is to communicate real ideas clearly, naturally, and with a recognisable perspective.

lessons.title: Tuesday's Goal
lessons.content:
By the end of today's lesson, you should have a clearer understanding of what a writing voice is, how it differs from tone, and how different styles of writing can help you communicate ideas in different ways.

You should also begin recognising the difference between writing that merely sounds polished and writing that communicates something specific, meaningful, and recognisably human.

As you continue developing your skills, don't become so concerned with sounding like a professional writer that you lose sight of what you actually want to say.

Learn the rules. Study writers you admire. Experiment with different approaches. Practise consistently. Then pay attention to what feels natural, what works for your audience, and what makes your writing distinct.

You do not need to discover your final writing voice today. You need to begin paying attention to it. Your voice develops every time you write, reflect, revise, and try again.

And remember, this is your final week of probation. The assessment will test your understanding of the work covered across both weeks, and you need at least 60% to progress.

Take these lessons seriously. Practise what you've learned. Don't settle for simply watching the videos.

Learn to write well. Then learn to write in a way that only you can.
